implementerProof.how: I re-ran both of the implementer's proofs that name a production-like surface, independently and from my own fixtures. Proof 1 (acceptance 2, `legion workspace-init provision` with the issue branch merged and deleted): re-built the binary from the workspace at b650d854, built my own bare remote and feed mirror, deleted refs/heads/legion/ACME-1 from both, and got the same result it reports — exit 0, `workspace-init: … on legion/ACME-1 from main`, a.txt alone in the workspace, .jj/legion-created written. I then drove the same command against a mirror of sjawhar/legion itself, which it did not: 4.8 s, 148 MB, the workspace on legion/INFRA-80 at main's 7bf2759 with the branch deleted from the feed and on the issue's own pushed head b650d854 with it present. Proof 3 (acceptance 5, `legion start --check-config`): staged the example's three token files, two App PEMs and a kubeconfig myself and reproduced both its outcomes, then broke the key five more ways (see the proof entry). Proof 4 (acceptance 5, the deletion grep): re-ran it at the code head and read all 17 hits — each is a changelog, a contract note recording what 36 removed, a deliberate statement that the thing is gone, or a negative assertion in the live proofs; none is an implementation. Proof 2 (acceptance 1) is a `go test` over rendered goldens against the pinned Agent Sandbox CRD, which is a regression lock and not a proof of a criterion on a production-like surface; rather than reject the round for it I drove the same claim on a real Kubernetes cluster myself, in proof entry 1 below, and the architect's standing decision (its message of 05:23Z) is that the Agent Sandbox controller's own pass-through is the live Stage 4a run's to judge and is recorded unproven, not failed.

proof.criterion: 1. No disk outlives a pod. The disk a pod is given is created with it and deleted with it, at the size and on the storage used today, and it is found by its name, which is the pod's with `-issue` after it, and by its pod owner, since Kubernetes keeps no labels on a disk of this kind.
proof.surface: A real Kubernetes cluster. The build namespace this worker pod may submit Jobs to admits exactly the volume shape this change renders for an issue pod — a new filesystem generic ephemeral volume of a scratch storage class whose claim template carries no labels or annotations — so I ran a pod declaring the same `spec.volumes[].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate` the goldens show (`testdata/golden/worker.json`: metadata {}, ReadWriteOnce, the operator's class, the operator's size), with the namespace's claim counter as the observation Legion's own tests cannot make.
proof.command: kubectl apply -f (Job infra-80-disk-cc8c2e: gvisor, one 4-CPU container, one ephemeral 20Gi claim template with empty metadata), then `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.volumes[0]}'`, `kubectl logs`, `kubectl get resourcequota builds -o jsonpath='{.status.used.<scratch class>.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/persistentvolumeclaims}'` polled through the pod's life, and `kubectl delete job infra-80-disk-cc8c2e`
proof.observed: The claim counter went 0 → 1 while the pod was still Pending, so the claim is created with the pod and not with the container. The pod's own spec carried the template back unchanged. At first mount the disk held `lost+found` alone, 19.5G free of a 20Gi claim, and took a 16 MiB write. The counter stayed at 1 after the pod reached Completed, so the claim's life is the pod object's, not the container's — which is why Legion's suspend, which deletes the pod, is what deletes the disk. After `kubectl delete job`, the pod was gone at the first poll and the counter was back to 0 at the next, about one second later; `kubectl get jobs,pods` then showed nothing of the run. This is the mechanism the change rests on, exercised on a real cluster of this deployment.
proof.negativeControl: The same Job with one label (`legion.dev/issue: infra-80`) on that claim template, submitted server-side with nothing created: refused — `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'build-jobs' … denied request: … a new filesystem ephemeral volume … whose claim template has no labels or annotations …`. A second enforcement point, independent of the pinned CRD's pruning, reaching the implementer's conclusion that a disk of this kind carries no labels and is found by its name and its pod owner instead.
proof.doesNotSettle: That the Agent Sandbox controller hands an ephemeral pod volume through to the pod untouched. No pod here can reach that controller (`kubectl auth can-i` answers no to every Sandbox and PersistentVolumeClaim verb available to this identity), so the live Stage 4a run against this head remains its judge, as the architect directed at 05:23Z and confirmed at 05:40Z.

proof.criterion: 2. An issue whose branch has been merged and deleted starts its agents.
proof.surface: The real `legion workspace-init provision` binary — the pod's second init container — built from the workspace at b650d854 (whose only difference from a5e26319 is the implement handoff file), run against a real bare git remote and a real feed mirror, and then against a mirror of sjawhar/legion itself with this issue's own branch deleted from the feed.
proof.command: `legion workspace-init provision --issue INFRA-80 --repo sjawhar/legion --default-branch main --root /tmp/big/root2 --credential-helper '!legion git-credential' --feed /tmp/big/feed` after `git --git-dir=/tmp/big/feed/sjawhar/legion.git update-ref -d refs/heads/legion/INFRA-80`; and the same against a two-commit fixture repository as ACME-1
proof.observed: Exit 0 in 4.8 s on a 5,868-ref repository, `workspace-init: /tmp/big/root2/workspaces/sjawhar/legion/infra-80 on legion/INFRA-80 from main`, the workspace's parent commit main's own 7bf2759c6e17 and `.jj/legion-created` stamped at the provision. The fixture run behaved the same and held a.txt alone, so the deleted branch's file was not carried. The provision never looks for a disk it left behind, and the failure that stopped six issues cannot arise from a branch GitHub deleted.
proof.negativeControl: The same command with refs/heads/legion/INFRA-80 still in the feed put the workspace's parent at b650d854, the issue's own pushed head, rather than at main — so the deleted-branch run read the deletion rather than never looking for a branch at all.

proof.criterion: 5. The file record store is no longer a choice under Kubernetes: a deployment cannot keep sessions as files on a disk that dies with its pod.
proof.surface: The real `legion start --check-config` CLI against `deploy/kubernetes/daemon/legion.yaml.example` with its three token files, two App PEMs and a kubeconfig staged by me, and LEGION_POSTGRES_DSN in the environment.
proof.command: `legion start --check-config --config legion.yaml` on the example, then on seven variants: session_store `pvc` with session_dsn_secret removed; session_store omitted entirely; `postgres` with session_dsn_secret removed; `Postgres`; `pvc` with the secret still named; an empty session_store; and an empty session_dsn_secret
proof.observed: The example exits 0 (`Config OK: project=WIDGETS`). Every way of not naming postgres exits 1 with one message — `runtime.kubernetes.session_store must be 'postgres': an issue pod's disk is deleted with the pod, so a session kept as a file on it ('pvc') dies with it and the next launch's resume fails on the missing file, retiring the claim after three failures` — including the omitted key, the wrong case, the empty string and `pvc` with the secret still present, so there is no spelling that slips a file store past the loader. `postgres` without the key exits 1 naming the key; an empty key exits 1 saying it must not be empty.
proof.negativeControl: The unmodified example, which names postgres and its secret, exits 0 — so the refusal is the store's and not a broken fixture.

proof.criterion: 5. No code is left that reuses, repairs or inspects a disk from an earlier pod, with the stale git-lock sweep kept for the retry on the same disk.
proof.surface: The tree at the code head, and the one runtime surface where a provision can still meet a non-empty disk: the kubelet restarts a failed init container in the same pod (the pod template's restartPolicy is Always, `manifest.go:377`), so a first attempt killed part-way leaves its work for the retry on the same disk.
proof.command: `grep -rn 'LEGION_EXPECT_ISSUE_VOLUME\|WorkspaceLost\|workspace-recovered\|hasRetainedSession\|IssueHasSessions\|ensureCloneConnectivity\|mark-lost' packages docs scripts` re-run at the code head; then `legion workspace-init provision` a second and a third time into a root it had already provisioned, once after planting this issue's own production failure signature in the clone (`refs/jj/keep/badref` naming a commit the clone does not hold)
proof.observed: 17 hits, each a changelog, a contract note in `internal/api/version.go` recording what contract 36 removed, a deliberate statement that the thing is gone (`docs/kubernetes.md:723`, the sessions-import runbook), or a negative assertion in the live proofs; no implementation. A plain second provision on the same root exits 0. With the planted bad ref, it exits 1 at once (0.98 s) with `fatal: bad object refs/jj/keep/badref` — it attempts no repair, does not hang and does not half-succeed, which is what leaves the pod replaceable: a failed init container is `Observation.InitFailed`, `relaunch` reads `live=false` and replaces the pod, and the replacement brings a disk of its own. The weeks-long version of that failure is structurally gone; what is left is one pod replacement.
proof.negativeControl: The one repair the spec says stays: with four stale git locks planted instead of the bad ref (`index.lock`, `config.lock`, `HEAD.lock`, `refs/heads/main.lock`), the same command removed each one by name — `workspace-init: removed the stale git lock …, last written 0s ago` — and exited 0. So the sweep that must stay works and the repair that must be gone is gone.

proof.criterion: 6. Nothing is left behind at the cutover — the upgrade half: an issue_suspend row the running release queued must still run after the daemon is upgraded, or its issue's lifecycle lane stalls on a row no retry can finish.
proof.surface: A real PostgreSQL 16, brought up as a workload in the cluster and reached by its Service name from this pod, carrying the daemon's own schema and driven by the daemon's own migration runner (`store.Open`/`store.Migrate`) and its own enqueue path (`record.Postgres.Enqueue`), with the payload bytes produced by `json.Marshal` of `record.IssueSuspend` exactly as the release before this change declares it, `release` tag and all.
proof.command: A Go program built against the module at this head: open the database, migrate it, delete the schema_version row for 51 so it stands where a deployment on the running release stands, enqueue the two rows that release writes (a child's close as done with `"release":true` and a keeping close without the key, one of them mid-retry with attempts 2 and a future next_at), decode each with `record.DecodeOutboxPayload`, then run `store.Migrate` again as the upgrade does and decode again
proof.observed: At schema 50 the head binary refuses the releasing row — `decode outbox row 1: json: unknown field "release"` — which is the stall the migration exists to prevent, reproduced rather than argued. The upgrade's migration run applied exactly 1 migration and left schema_version 51. Both rows then decode: `{"tree":"ACME-208","generation":3,"treeGeneration":7}` as `record.IssueSuspend{Tree:"ACME-208", Generation:3, TreeGeneration:7}`, and the keeping row unchanged. Every other column of both rows is byte-identical before and after — attempts 2, next_at, last_error and created_at — so a row in the middle of its retry backoff keeps it.
proof.negativeControl: The keeping row, which the release wrote without the key (`release` carries omitempty): the head binary decoded it before the migration and the migration left it untouched, so the update's `payload ? 'release'` guard selects the rows that need it and nothing else.

ciAtCodeHead.note: Read, not re-run. Lint, types and every unit and integration suite are CI's, including the packages this pod cannot run (./internal/daemon, ./internal/admit, ./internal/intake, ./internal/natsauth, ./internal/testnats, ./internal/runtime/tmux) and the daemon tests the spec names as acceptance 3's proof. I waited for no lane and re-ran none as evidence.

notReachedHere: Acceptance 1's cluster half and acceptance 4 in full — that the Agent Sandbox controller passes an ephemeral pod volume through to the pod untouched, and that an agent resumes from the session database into a replacement pod. The missing surface is a cluster running the Agent Sandbox controller with a Legion daemon against it: this pod may create Jobs and Services in a build namespace but holds no Sandbox or PersistentVolumeClaim verb anywhere. The live Stage 4a run against this head is the judge; the architect has it and had no result at 05:40Z, and directed me not to hold the round for it.

Acceptance 3's three cases (a paused issue, an issue handed to a new tree, an issue whose pod dies mid-turn) — daemon-level orchestration the spec itself names daemon tests as the proof of, and those tests need a Postgres or a container runtime the CI lane has and this pod's go test invocation does not reach. Two halves of it I did reach on real surfaces: a fresh disk provisions from the issue's pushed branch (proof 2), and `.jj/legion-created` is stamped at every provision, which is what `launcher.resumable` compares the session's last write against to set LEGION_WORKSPACE_RECREATED — so on a disk that is always new the notice is always true.
Acceptance 6's cutover and the six named issues — a person's reading of a deployment, not an agent's.
residualRisks: An issue pod's name is stable, so its generic ephemeral claim is always named <pod>-issue. A relaunch creates the replacement pod after awaitPodGone, which waits for the pod and not for the claim the garbage collector reaps after it; a replacement pod created inside that window stays Pending until the predecessor's claim is gone. Measured on a real cluster: about one second from the pod's deletion to the claim leaving the namespace's quota, against a 120 s boot timeout, and `waitedOut` now prints a Pending pod's events so the wait names itself. The architect accepted this as a risk at 05:40Z.

Every pod start now depends on the repository cache, and a production check's wake up to fourteen days after the merge may find the cache swept (retain_hours 168). The provision itself is cheap — 4.8 s and 148 MB for sjawhar/legion from a local feed, against a 30-minute CloneTimeout and a 70-minute FetchBudget — so the exposure is the cold clone the cache's own rebuild pays, not the clone the issue pays.
observations: `workspaceInit` still creates `<root>/sessions` on the issue's disk (`cmd/legion/workspace_init.go:177`), and nothing mounts it any more: the role containers' sessions subPath mount is deleted in this change, and `SessionsSubPath` survives only for `legion sessions import --tree-volume`, which reads a stopped legion-v10.0.0 deployment's tree volume. The simplify pass removed the controller's identical mkdir and left the issue pod's. Nothing a user meets breaks, so it is not a failure and I wrote no test to pin it; it is dead state on every issue's disk and the reviewer may want it gone.

Found while using the cluster for this round, outside this issue: `docs/kubernetes.md`'s "Running a workload in the cluster from a role" is stale since dispatch://INFRA-206 was applied — all three permission checks now answer yes where it says two answer no, the Service half it records as never executed and Forbidden now runs, and the Service manifest it publishes (`selector: {job-name: …}`) is refused by the applied admission policy, which requires the owning Job's controller-uid. Evidence at dispatch://INFRA-49/comment/861d759f-0834-4bfb-8941-4800d062158d; the Legion controller resolved the ask and gave the fix to dispatch://INFRA-71's tree, which owns that section.
